The opera enters a second act. You get up at intermission, return the rabbit and receive a look of profound betrayal.

events.title: The Duck Was Too Big
events.text: 2:12 AM. A real scream, then sobbing: "The duck was too big." You don't know which duck. You will never know which duck.

choices.label: Go in and hold them until it passes

outcomes.text: You hold them in the dark and say "no ducks, no ducks" until their breathing slows. You have never been so sure what you're for.
They fall asleep instantly, in the shape of a starfish with knees. Your partner takes a heel to the kidney at 4. You take one to the ear at 5.
Your partner is up before you finish nudging. Through the wall: "I'll talk to the duck." Nobody has ever been braver.
Your partner nudges you back. You nudge harder. This is how wars start. You go, because the crying is louder than the principle.

events.title: "Is It Morning?"
events.text: 4:52 AM. A small, bright voice: "Is it morning?" It is not morning. It is a number that should not exist. They are standing up, holding a shoe. Where did they get a shoe?

outcomes.text: You say it nine times in the same flat voice, like a very patient airline. On the tenth, they lie down. You don't, because your body has decided it's a workday.
Your partner takes the early shift without a word. At 5:01 you hear them downstairs, whispering a book about diggers. You love them very much right now.
"Your turn for mornings," they murmur, and roll over. Is it? You can't remember. Neither can they. You go, holding the shoe.
Somehow it works. They talk quietly to the shoe for twenty minutes and fall back asleep holding it. You will never know why.
"Is it morning?" becomes "IT'S MORNING," which is not a question. You get up. It is, technically, morning now.

events.title: False Alarm
events.text: 1:40 AM. The monitor crackles. A sigh, a rustle, one small cough. You're upright with one foot on the cold floor. Then nothing. Then more nothing.

outcomes.text: You lie back down. You trust it. It turns out to be trustworthy. It's the best thing that will happen to you all day.
"Hear what?" your partner whispers. "Exactly," you say. You both lie there grinning in the dark, like you got away with something.

events.title: The Midnight Concert
events.text: 11:48 PM. The toddler who wasn't sleepy at bedtime is still not sleepy. They're giving a concert in the crib. Song 9 is called "Truck." So was song 4.

choices.label: Go in and be the most boring person alive

outcomes.text: You sit in the dark and describe your tax return in a monotone. By the deductions, they're out. You've never been so proud of being dull.
Your partner goes in and does the slow-blink-and-hum thing they're weirdly good at. Silence in six minutes. You'd be jealous if you weren't already asleep.
"You did bedtime," your partner whispers. "This is your encore." Harsh, but accurate. You go in to a standing ovation from one.

choices.label: Let the concert run its course

outcomes.text: Song 14 trails off in the middle of "Truck." They fell asleep singing, which is how you'd like to go too.
The second wind gets a second wind. At 12:40 you go in, defeated, and they greet you like a fan who got backstage.

events.title: Wired
events.text: 1:30 AM. The toddler is asleep. Your partner is asleep. You are lying perfectly still, vibrating at the exact frequency of a 4 PM coffee.

choices.label: You're up anyway. Take the next wake-up.

outcomes.text: At 2:10 the monitor crackles and you're there in nine seconds, like a firefighter who was already at the fire. Your partner wakes up suspiciously rested.

choices.label: Empty the dishwasher in the dark

outcomes.text: You put away 31 things by feel. Two go in the wrong drawer and will confuse your partner for weeks. The kitchen is clean. You are still awake.

choices.label: Catch up on the group chat

outcomes.text: You vote in the pajama-day poll, answer a six-day-old bake sale question and send a thumbs-up at 1:34 AM. Someone replies, "are you ok?"

events.title: The Molar, Live
events.text: 1:15 AM. The molar is still coming in, and it wants everyone to know. Your toddler is gnawing the crib rail and crying in a key you didn't know existed.

choices.label: Cold washcloth, rocking chair, the long haul

outcomes.text: Forty minutes in the chair. They chew the washcloth, then your sleeve, then fall asleep mid-chew. Your arm is dead. Your heart is weirdly full.

choices.label: Give the dose on the pediatrician's chart

outcomes.text: Kitchen light on. You read the chart twice and measure with the syringe, not a spoon. Twenty minutes later the crying winds down to a hum.
Your partner takes the shift. Through the wall you hear them humming a song about a tooth that they are clearly making up as they go. Verse three is ambitious.
"I did the last molar," your partner whispers. There have been four molars. You decide not to audit this at 1 AM. You go.

events.title: "Corduroy Man?"
events.text: 3:02 AM. "Corduroy man?" your toddler asks the dark. The man in corduroy is not available. He is, presumably, asleep somewhere in a lot of corduroy.

choices.label: Go in and sing his song yourself

outcomes.text: You whisper the whole theme song. You know every word. You know the key change. You never chose this knowledge. They sigh, satisfied, and sleep.
Your partner goes in and does the corduroy man's voice, perfectly. You didn't know they could do that. You'll be thinking about it for days.
"Your show, your shift," your partner mumbles. You did put it on at 4 PM. You go.
A long pause. "Corduroy man sleeping," they repeat, gravely, and lie down out of professional courtesy.
"CORDUROY MAN WAKE UP," they announce, which wakes everyone except the corduroy man. You go in.

events.title: The Sandwich Photo
events.text: Your partner texts a photo of their lunch. A sandwich, eaten with two hands, sitting down, in a room with a door. "How's your day? 😊"

choices.label: Reply with a photo of the toddler in a colander

outcomes.text: Staging it takes ten minutes and a bribe. They reply with fourteen crying-laughing faces. For a second, you're on the same team.
Sent. It feels incredible for four seconds. Then three dots appear, disappear, and never come back.

choices.label: Don't reply. Eat crusts over the sink.

outcomes.text: You eat four crusts and half a cheese stick, standing up. A feast. They'll see "Read 12:14" and wonder.

events.title: Who's More Tired
events.text: "So tired today 😩," your partner texts at 2:12 PM. You have been awake since 5:14. You have many thoughts, and all of them are numbers.

outcomes.text: It costs you something to send it. They reply with a heart and "you too, I know you're wiped." That costs them something too.

choices.label: Send your wake time, step count and a photo of the ceiling

outcomes.text: 5:14 AM, 11,402 steps and yogurt on the ceiling. Undefeated. They don't reply. You've won, and you're alone with the trophy.
A handshake emoji arrives. 🤝 It isn't a hug, but it isn't a scoreboard either.

events.title: The Scoreboard
events.text: "I did bath last night," your partner texts, unprompted, in response to nothing. The scoreboard is open. Someone is keeping it.

outcomes.text: "Thank you" takes you nine tries to type without an edge. It lands. "I just wanted you to know," they write. They did.

choices.label: "And I did the last four mornings."

outcomes.text: "Wasn't a competition." "Then why did you bring it up?" You both put your phones face-down, in different buildings, at the same time.
They scroll. They go quiet. "Okay. Tonight's mine." You were right, which is less fun than it sounds.
They scroll. It's even. Actually, it leans their way. "Interesting document," they reply. You delete the ledger app, then reinstall it.

events.title: Unprompted
events.text: Your partner texts, out of nowhere: "You're doing a great job. I know today's a lot." No emoji. No request attached. Just the words, sitting there.

choices.label: Say it back, and mean it

outcomes.text: "So are you. Thank you for saying it." You read the thread twice. Then a third time, in the bathroom, with the door locked.

choices.label: Screenshot it for the hard days

outcomes.text: You save it in a photo album called "Proof." Next to it: the ultrasound, and a picture of a perfect nap.
"Nothing. I just meant it." You feel like a jerk, then a little less like one when they send a heart anyway.
"...The good spatula. But I still meant it." You laugh out loud in the cereal aisle. Fair trade.

events.title: "Where Did You Put It?"
events.text: Your partner texts: "Where did you put the daycare backpack?" The "you" is doing a lot of work. You put it in their car last night, so they could find it.

outcomes.text: You apologize for a thing you did correctly. "Found it, thanks!" Peace, purchased at full price.

choices.label: "Where YOU put it. In YOUR car."

outcomes.text: Capital letters. Two sets. It's satisfying in the exact way that makes the evening worse.
They find the backpack, then the ledger. They go quiet, then take two of your rows for the weekend without being asked.
The ledger shows they packed it the last three days. You found one backpack. They found the receipts.

events.title: The Empty Carton
events.text: The milk carton is in the fridge. It is empty. Someone put an empty carton back, and there are two suspects, and one of them can't reach the fridge.

choices.label: Let it go. Black coffee it is.

outcomes.text: You drink it black. You are an adult. You are, at most, 15% bitter about it, and the coffee is 85%.

choices.label: Text a photo of the carton. No caption.

outcomes.text: No caption needed. The photo says everything. Their reply, "lol sorry," says less.

choices.label: Open the ledger to the groceries column

outcomes.text: "...I'll get milk." They get milk. They also get the good cookies. An apology in snack form.
They reply with photos of the last four grocery receipts. All theirs. You drink the coffee black, as penance.

events.title: "Who Taught Them That?"
events.text: Your partner calls on speaker. The toddler grabs the phone and says "[BLEEP]" with crisp, professional diction. A pause. Then: "Who taught them that?"

outcomes.text: You confess. They laugh, then admit they said it in traffic on Sunday. A joint custody of the word.
"I don't swear in the car." You both know what happens at the merge onto the highway. Neither of you says so.

choices.label: Make a crackling noise. "You're breaking up!"

outcomes.text: "Krrrsh." It's not convincing. You hang up. The toddler says the word again, to the toaster.

events.title: Running 20 Late
events.text: "Running 20 late, sorry!!" Two exclamation points. You know what two exclamation points cost. You've sent them yourself.

outcomes.text: Two exclamation points back. The universal sign of a parent doing their best. Twenty minutes is forty, but you knew that.
The period lands like a dropped plate. They'll be home in twenty minutes, already apologizing.
They walk in with dumplings and a guilty face. You'd take this deal every night of the week.
They forget. They walk in with apologies and a work bag, and nothing that can be eaten.

events.title: Calendar Tetris
events.text: "Can you do pickup Thursday? I have a thing." Their Thursday thing is a work dinner. Your Thursday thing is pickup. All of your things are pickup.

outcomes.text: "You're the best." You are. It's on the calendar now, in your color, next to all your other things in your color.
"What thing?" You invent a dentist. You'll have to go to the dentist now. This is how lies work.
"Deal." They take bedtime tonight. You do Thursday. A fair trade, negotiated by two people who used to talk about books.
"Two? It's one pickup." Talks collapse. You get Thursday anyway, and a reputation as a hostage-taker.

events.title: The Dishwasher Doctrine
events.text: Your partner is reloading the dishwasher you just loaded. Silently. Correcting it. Every bowl they move is a small, wordless essay about you.

choices.label: Ask them to teach you their system

outcomes.text: They light up. There's a system. It has a philosophy. Bowls face the center, "like a congregation." You learn it. You'll never use it.

choices.label: "There's no wrong way to load a dishwasher."

outcomes.text: "There are many wrong ways. You found a new one." You leave the room. The bowls stay where they put them.

choices.label: Show them the dishes column of the ledger

outcomes.text: They look at the ledger, then at the bowl in their hand. They put the bowl back exactly where you had it.
The dishes column is mostly theirs. They keep loading. You go fold something, quietly, with dignity.

events.title: The Handoff: Running on Fumes
events.text: Your partner walks in and finds you lying on the kitchen floor while the toddler drives a toy truck up and down your back. "Hi," you tell the floor.

outcomes.text: They take the toddler. You take the stairs one at a time, like an old dog, and lie face-down on the bed. Ten minutes. Glorious.

choices.label: "I'm fine." Get up and start dinner.

outcomes.text: You are not fine. You make pasta anyway. They watch you salt the water three times and say nothing, which is its own kindness.

choices.label: Tell them the truth: you're running on fumes

outcomes.text: "I'm running on fumes." They sit down on the floor next to you. The toddler drives the truck over both of you. Nobody gets up for a while.

events.title: The Handoff: "I'm Wrecked."
events.text: Your partner walks in, drops their bag and says, "I'm wrecked." By your count you've done four more things than them this week. You have counted. You are always counting.

outcomes.text: You let the count go, for tonight. They sit. They look at you like you're someone they'd like to marry, which, technically, happened.

choices.label: Read them the count, out loud

outcomes.text: Mornings, dishes, the forms, the snack bag. They listen. They say "okay." The okay has a temperature, and it's cold.
They know the count too. They take the toddler without a word. You take a shower long enough to legally count as a bath.
They take the toddler with a sigh you'll hear in your dreams. You take the ten minutes anyway. They were owed. You think.

events.title: Eye-Level Marketing
events.text: The checkout lane. Candy at exactly toddler height, wrapped in a cartoon with enormous eyes. Your toddler has spotted it. Your toddler is drawing a long, theatrical breath.

outcomes.text: $1.89 for eleven minutes of peace. A parent in the next lane clocks the candy and says nothing, loudly.
They consider an appeal, then wave at a stranger instead. A parent in the next lane gives you a small, respectful nod.
The breath comes out. All of it. A man buying a single lime turns around, slowly, to watch.

choices.label: Make it a game: find something red

outcomes.text: The gum, the exit sign, the cashier's lanyard, your eyes. They find nine red things and forget the candy ever existed.

events.title: The Sugar Crash
events.text: Forty-five minutes after the candy, the bill arrives. Your toddler has gone from rocket to puddle and is weeping because their sock is "too sock."

outcomes.text: Twenty minutes on the hallway floor, mourning the sock. You sit beside them and mourn something too. Possibly your twenties.
Crackers stop the crash halfway down. The crumbs go everywhere, which you'll also pay for. Everything in this house is on credit.
You put on a song and dance like an uncle at a wedding. They join in, sobbing, then laughing, then lying very still on your foot.

events.title: Just Lie Down for a Minute
events.text: Dinner is over. The dishes are a tower. Your partner is wiping down the high chair. The couch is right there, humming a song only you can hear.

choices.label: Lie down. Just for a minute.

outcomes.text: You lie down for a minute. The minute lasts twenty. It is the best minute you've had all month.
You wash. You stack. You narrate your own sacrifice in your head, in the voice of a nature documentary.
You wash, they dry. Neither of you mentions the toddler. It feels like a small, damp date.

events.title: Very Loud Dishes
events.text: You open your eyes to the sound of your partner doing the dishes. Loudly. Each plate goes down like a closing argument. The minute is over.

choices.label: Get up, grab a towel, say thank you

outcomes.text: "Thanks for doing these." "Mm." You dry in silence. The silence is itemized.

choices.label: "I was up at five with them."

outcomes.text: "I was up at five too. Then I went to work." A pan goes into the rack with real feeling. Nobody wins this one.

choices.label: Stay horizontal. Commit to the bit.

outcomes.text: You keep your eyes shut. They know you're awake. You know they know. The dishes get done, and filed, and remembered.

events.title: "Playground?"
events.text: Your toddler is holding your shoes and pointing at the door. "Playground?" It is drizzling. You are wearing one sock.

outcomes.text: "Later" works like a spell. They put the shoes down. You sit. You have just taken out a loan at a terrible rate.
Slide, wet bench, slide, for forty-five minutes. Their cheeks go pink. You stand by the swings holding a coffee like a mob lieutenant.
They drop the shoes and go bother a block tower. You suspect a trap. There is no trap. You fold an entire load of laundry.
They lie face-down on the doormat in protest. A sit-in. They are a very small union.

events.title: "Later" Is Now
events.text: Two hours ago you said "later." Your toddler did not forget. Your toddler never forgets. They're at the door in one shoe and your hat. "IT'S LATER."

outcomes.text: You go, now tired, now cold, now later. They don't care. They run to the slide like it's an old friend. Worth it, barely.
"You SAID." They're right. You did. This meltdown has the moral high ground, and it knows it.
"Later later" buys you ninety more minutes. They empty the shoe rack in protest. Your credit score with this toddler is now in the low hundreds.

events.title: Fourteen People Ahead of You
events.text: The post office. Fourteen people ahead of you, one window open. Your toddler has started licking the rope barrier and introducing themselves to a stranger's bag.

outcomes.text: Silence, instantly. The woman behind you mouths "same." The line moves. Nobody has to know what it cost yet.
A stamp, a sad plant, a man holding nine identical boxes. By the window they're narrating for the whole line. Two people clap.

choices.label: Abandon the line. Mail it never.

outcomes.text: You leave. The package rides home in the stroller basket, where it will live for another week, judging you.

events.title: You Need Your Phone Back
events.text: In fifteen minutes they have changed your phone's language to Finnish, taken 212 photos of their own nostril and texted your boss a single "p." They will not be returning it.

choices.label: Take it back. Brace for impact.

outcomes.text: You pry it loose. The scream has a bridge and a key change. Everyone nearby is now a witness.
You hold out your hand. They hand it over. Just like that. A stranger looks at you like you're a wizard. You will never understand them.
Five more minutes. You both know what five more minutes is. It's a down payment on the same fight.

choices.label: Trade it for your car keys

outcomes.text: The keys are accepted after a review period. You get the phone back, sticky forever. The keys vanish. You find them forty minutes later in a boot.

events.title: The Late-Afternoon Cookie
events.text: A cookie has been requested, with "please," which is new and devastating. Dinner is about an hour away. Every parenting book you own is watching from the shelf.

outcomes.text: Eaten in four seconds, crumbs spread evenly across the house. They hug your leg. You feel like a genius. The feeling has a due date.
"After dinner," they repeat solemnly, like a contract. They will hold you to it. They are a small lawyer.
They take the news badly: a slow slide down the fridge door, then the floor, then a long stare at you from under the table.

choices.label: Apple slices, served like a fancy restaurant

outcomes.text: You fan the slices on a plate and call it "the tasting menu." They eat three and pretend the fourth is a phone. It counts.

events.title: Full of Cookie
events.text: Dinner happened near your toddler, not to them. One noodle, licked and returned. The cookie got there first. Now, an hour before bed, they are starving.

outcomes.text: Toast, banana, cheese cubes: a second dinner, served by a chef who is also the dishwasher. They eat all of it. Of course they do.
The kitchen is closed. The customer is not satisfied. The customer lies on the kitchen floor and files a complaint at full volume.

choices.label: Another cookie. You've come this far.

outcomes.text: Cookie number two, an hour before bed. They're vibrating at a frequency that rattles the windows. Bedtime will be a negotiation with a hummingbird.

events.title: Just Resting My Eyes
events.text: 3 PM, the dead zone. Your toddler is next to you on the couch, "reading" a board book upside down, out loud. You could close your eyes. Just to listen better.

choices.label: Close your eyes. Just for a minute.

outcomes.text: You are not asleep. You are listening with your eyes closed. You are listening so hard you drool a little.

choices.label: Get up. Walk around the block together.

outcomes.text: Cold air, one stick, a very important leaf. You come back more awake than you left. They come back sleepier. Everyone wins.
The third coffee of the day tastes like a decision you'll revisit at 1 AM.

events.title: The Couch Hangover
events.text: The little rest is billing you. Your head is full of wet sand, a couch seam is printed across your cheek, and your body is now certain it's bedtime. It is not bedtime.

choices.label: Cold water on your face. Push through.

outcomes.text: Cold water, a head shake, a pep talk in the mirror. You get through the afternoon at about 60% of a person.
Coffee at 4 PM. The fog lifts. You can already hear it at 1 AM, knocking politely on the inside of your skull.
You lie back down. Your toddler narrates the living room's destruction like a sports announcer. The cushions are gone. You hear the word "glitter."

events.title: Theo's Party: Yes / No / Maybe
events.text: The invite for Theo's party has been open in a browser tab since last week. Saturday, 10 AM, a trampoline place with a cartoon kangaroo on the sign. The buttons say Yes, No and Maybe.

outcomes.text: "Yes! See you there! 🎉" One click. You feel like an adult who handles things, at least until Saturday at 10.

choices.label: Ask your partner to handle it

outcomes.text: "Done. Also bought the gift. It's a kazoo." A kazoo. For someone else's child. Your partner is a quiet genius.
"Which Theo?" There's only one Theo. The tab stays open, glowing at you.

choices.label: Later. Maybe is still an option.

outcomes.text: Maybe is always an option. Maybe is how adults say "I haven't checked with my toddler's nap."

events.title: The Form on the Fridge
events.text: The daycare field-trip form is on the fridge, under a magnet, under a drawing of either you or a potato. It needs a signature, an emergency contact and "any additional notes."

outcomes.text: Signature, phone number, and under "additional notes" you write "bites when bored" and then cross it out. Into the backpack. Done.

choices.label: Text your partner to sign it at drop-off

outcomes.text: A photo arrives: the form, signed, being handed to a teacher. Your partner has never looked more attractive.
"What form?" The one on the fridge. The one with the potato. It stays on the fridge.

choices.label: Later. It's a form. Forms keep.

outcomes.text: Forms keep. Pumpkin patches, it turns out, do not.

events.title: Press 9 for More Options
events.text: The rash is still there. The pediatrician's phone tree has nine options, none of which is "rash," and hold music that is a pan flute cover of a song you used to love.

outcomes.text: Option 4, then 2, then a nurse named Pat who says, kindly, "send a photo, it sounds like eczema." Fragrance-free cream twice a day. You could cry.

choices.label: Ask your partner to call on their break

outcomes.text: They call from a stairwell at work. "Eczema. Cream twice a day. Nurse Pat says hi." You don't know a Nurse Pat. You love Nurse Pat.
"Can't, back-to-backs all day." The rash and the phone tree are both still yours.
It's probably fine. You look at it every eleven minutes for the rest of the day, just to check that it's fine.

events.title: The Books by the Door
events.text: The library books are stacked by the door, where they've been since Monday, becoming furniture. The library closes at 6. One of them is about a bear who is also tired.

choices.label: Return them now. Make it an outing.

outcomes.text: The drop slot eats the books one at a time while your toddler waves goodbye to each. They pick out three new ones. The cycle continues.

choices.label: Ask your partner to drop them on the way home

outcomes.text: They take the bag without a sigh. That evening: "Returned. The librarian says the bear book is very popular."
They forget the bag by the door. The books remain furniture. The bear remains tired.
That's exactly the problem, but you don't think about it that way.
